lead: A memory macro is a core of identical cells wrapped in peripheral circuits: address decoders that pick a row and a column, sense amplifiers that read a tiny bitline swing, precharge circuits, write drivers and the timing control that sequences them. The core sets the density; the periphery sets the speed and much of the power. This chapter builds the architecture from the address bits outwards, sizes it with numbers, and explains the circuits examiners ask for: the predecoded row decoder, the column multiplexer and the latch sense amplifier.
prereq: You need: decoders and multiplexers from Chapter 4.5, and the SRAM and DRAM cells of Chapter 4.9.

blocks.text: Memories are classed by function (read-write SRAM and DRAM; non-volatile EPROM, EEPROM and flash; read-only ROM) and by access: random, serial (FIFO) or content-addressable (CAM), which returns the address of a stored word.

One word per row would make the array absurdly tall and its bitlines long and slow, so the array is folded to be roughly square. Each row holds 2<sup>c</sup> words side by side; the K address bits split into r row bits, which pick the wordline, and c column bits, which pick one word from that row:
N = 2K, rows = 2r, columns = M × 2c, K = r + c
Here N is the number of words, M the bits per word, K the number of address bits, r the row bits and c the column bits. Choosing r and c makes the array nearly square.

Large memories add a third level. The array is cut into blocks (banks), and block-address bits pick one block. Only that block's wordline and bitlines switch, so every wire is shorter, with less RC delay, and the power falls. The building blocks are always the same: the core array, the row and column decoders, precharge and equalise circuits, sense amplifiers, write drivers, input and output buffers and the timing control.

A row decoder for r bits raises one of 2<sup>r</sup> wordlines. Built directly, every wordline needs an r-input AND gate, and each address line, true or complement, drives half of all those gates. Predecoding splits the work: small decoders first decode groups of address bits, then a 2-input or 3-input gate per wordline combines one line from each group. For 10 row bits, two 5-to-32 predecoders make 64 lines, and each of the 1024 wordlines is a 2-input AND (a NAND followed by the wordline driver) of one line from each predecoder (worked example 1). The wide gates shrink, the load on each address line falls, and the final gate fits the narrow cell pitch.

The final stage is a wordline driver, sized to charge a long, heavily loaded wordline quickly; logical effort sizes the chain from address pin to wordline. Dynamic decoders precharge all outputs and discharge all but the selected one.

The column decoder picks one word's bitlines from the row. A pass-transistor column multiplexer connects one of 2<sup>c</sup> bitline pairs to each sense amplifier. A tree multiplexer needs fewer decoded select lines but puts c pass transistors in series; a one-level multiplexer puts only one transistor in series but needs a full c-to-2<sup>c</sup> column decoder. Before every access, precharge transistors pull each bitline pair to V<sub>DD</sub> (V<sub>DD</sub>/2 in DRAM) and an equalise transistor shorts BL to BLB so the pair starts exactly equal. For a write, the write driver pulls one bitline of the selected pair to 0.
A bitline carries hundreds of cells, so its capacitance C<sub>BL</sub> is large, while a cell's read current I<sub>cell</sub> is small. The time to build a swing ΔV is:

blocks.where: C<sub>BL</sub> is the bitline capacitance in F, ΔV the swing in V and I<sub>cell</sub> the cell read current in A. A full swing would take ten times as long as a 0.1 V one (worked example 2).

blocks.text: The sense amplifier needs only a small difference, about 0.1 V in SRAM or the tens of millivolts of a DRAM charge share, and amplifies it to full logic levels. The latch-type sense amplifier is a pair of cross-coupled inverters, the bistable loop of Chapter 4.6, connected to BL and BLB. With its enable off, the bitlines develop their difference; when the sense-enable signal SE turns on its tail transistor, positive feedback drives the higher side to VDD and the lower side to 0 within a few gate delays. The differential current-mirror amplifier is the other common type: slower to resolve, but it does not disturb the bitlines. DRAM uses the latch type on each folded bitline pair, which also writes the value back into the cell after the destructive read.

Timing control sequences precharge, wordline, sense enable and output latch. Many SRAMs make it self-timed: a replica bitline with dummy cells discharges like a real one, and its crossing fires SE, so the timing tracks process and temperature. Asynchronous SRAMs use address transition detection, the one-shot of Chapter 4.7, to start a cycle whenever any address bit changes. Spare rows and columns, switched in by fuses after test, repair faulty cells (see memory testing and memory fault models).

examples.question: A 1 Mbit SRAM is organised as 64K words × 16 bits. (a) How many address bits does it need? (b) Lay it out as a square 1024 × 1024 cell array: how many row and column address bits, and how wide is each column multiplexer? (c) Compare a direct row decoder with one built from two 5-to-32 predecoders, by the number of gate inputs and by the load on each address line.
steps: (a) 64K = 65536 = 2<sup>16</sup> words, so K = 16 address bits. Check: 65536 × 16 = 1048576 bits = 1 Mbit.
(b) 1024 rows = 2<sup>10</sup>, so r = 10. Each row has 1024 cells = M × 2<sup>c</sup> = 16 × 2<sup>c</sup>, so 2<sup>c</sup> = 64 and c = 6. Check: r + c = 10 + 6 = 16 = K.
Each of the 16 data bits has its own 64:1 column multiplexer and its own sense amplifier: 64 words share each row, one is picked.
(c) Direct: 1024 AND gates with 10 inputs each = 10240 gate inputs. Every address literal (A or A′) appears in half the gates, so it drives 512 gates.
Predecoded: two 5-to-32 predecoders have 64 five-input gates = 320 inputs, plus 1024 two-input gates = 2048 inputs, 2368 in all, about 4.3 times fewer.
Loads: each address literal now drives 16 of the 32 gates in its predecoder, and each predecoder line drives 32 wordline gates, instead of 512.
examples.answer: 16 address bits: 10 row bits for 1024 wordlines and 6 column bits for a 64:1 multiplexer on each of the 16 outputs. Predecoding needs 2368 gate inputs instead of 10240 and cuts the load on each address line from 512 gates to 16.

examples.question: An SRAM bitline has C<sub>BL</sub> = 100 fF and the cell read current is 40 µA. The sense amplifier needs ΔV = 100 mV. How long must the wordline be on before SE fires, and how long would a full 1.0 V swing take?
steps: Saving: 2.5 − 0.25 = 2.25 ns per read, ten times faster bitline sensing.
examples.answer: SE can fire after about 0.25 ns; waiting for a full swing would take 2.5 ns, so the sense amplifier saves 2.25 ns on every read.

traps: Taking the row count straight from the word count. A 64K × 16 memory is not 65536 rows; it is folded into, for example, 1024 rows of 64 words, with 10 row bits and 6 column bits.
Forgetting the word width when finding column bits: columns = M × 2<sup>c</sup>, so 1024 columns of 16-bit words give 2<sup>c</sup> = 64, not 1024.
Saying SRAM bitlines precharge to V<sub>DD</sub>/2. SRAM precharges to V<sub>DD</sub>; DRAM precharges to V<sub>DD</sub>/2.
Calling the column multiplexer a decoder. The column decoder makes the select lines; the multiplexer is the pass transistors they drive.

quiz.q: List the peripheral circuits around a memory core.
quiz.a: Row decoder and wordline drivers, column decoder and column multiplexer, precharge and equalise circuits, sense amplifiers, write drivers, input and output buffers, and timing control.

quiz.q: Why is a memory array folded to be roughly square?
quiz.a: A tall array of one word per row would have very long bitlines, with large capacitance and slow reads, and a huge row decoder. Putting several words in each row shortens the bitlines and balances wordline and bitline delays; column bits then pick the word.

quiz.q: How does predecoding help a row decoder?
quiz.a: It decodes small groups of address bits first, so each wordline needs only a 2- or 3-input gate instead of an r-input one. Gate inputs and the load on each address line both fall, and the final gate fits the cell pitch.

quiz.q: A 4 Mbit SRAM is organised as 256K × 16 in a square 2048 × 2048 array. Find the address bits, row bits, column bits and multiplexer width.
quiz.a: 256K = 2<sup>18</sup>, so K = 18. 2048 rows gives r = 11. 2048 columns = 16 × 2<sup>c</sup>, so 2<sup>c</sup> = 128 and c = 7, a 128:1 multiplexer per output bit. Check: 11 + 7 = 18.

quiz.q: A bitline of 150 fF is discharged by a 30 µA cell current. How long does a 120 mV swing take?
Why do SRAMs time the sense enable from a replica bitline instead of a fixed delay?
quiz.a: The bitline swing rate changes with process, voltage and temperature. A fixed delay must cover the slowest case and wastes time in the others, or fires too early. A replica bitline discharges like a real one, so SE fires just when enough swing exists in every corner.

beyond: Not for the exam. Memory compilers generate SRAM macros of any size with verified timing (OpenRAM is an open-source one), and modern SRAMs add read and write assist circuits for low supply voltages. Search next for "OpenRAM" and "SRAM read assist".
